analysis.one_liner: Lets merchants band together to negotiate lower credit and debit card processing fees.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Visa, Mastercard, and the banks behind them charge stores a fee on nearly every card swipe, and stores have had to accept whatever fee is set because antitrust law bars them from bargaining as a group. This bill would let merchants negotiate those fees jointly, and if negotiation failed, a panel of three judges would set the fee schedule at levels a competitive market would produce. It never moved after being sent to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants of every size—from small shops to national retailers—who pay a percentage of each card sale to the card networks and issuing banks. If those fees came down, some of the savings would likely reach shoppers through lower prices, since card fees are a cost of doing business built into what stores charge.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets merchants and payment-system providers jointly negotiate access fees, with limited antitrust immunity, because current law treats any group negotiation among competing merchants as illegal price-fixing [S3].

If providers and merchants cannot agree, three full-time Electronic Payment System Judges would set the fee schedule for two-year periods, choosing whichever of the two sides' final offers most closely matches what a competitive market would produce, based on the providers' actual costs and a normal rate of return [S3].
The largest issuers, acquirers, and card networks would have to disclose their itemized costs to run the system, information that is now closely held [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Card networks like Visa and Mastercard and the banks that issue their cards, which collect the swipe fee on every transaction and would see that revenue cut if fees dropped toward competitive levels. Some of the loss could be shifted to cardholders through higher annual fees or reduced rewards.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not directly regulate rates; it replaces one form of pricing with a government-supervised rate-setting process, and critics of such schemes argue judges may set fees at levels that do not reflect real market conditions [S3].

A general concern with capping merchant fees is that issuers can recoup lost interchange revenue from cardholders through higher annual fees, reduced rewards, or higher interest, shifting the cost from merchants to people who carry cards [S3].
Merchants are not required to pass savings along to customers, so some of the benefit could stay with retailers as added profit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings are real: interchange fees run into the tens of billions of dollars a year and are baked into consumer prices. But the design is a heavy lift—it creates a new federal panel of judges to run rate-setting proceedings every few years, and there is no guarantee banks would absorb the cut rather than raising cardholder fees. An honest supporter would concede the mechanism is complicated and the pass-through to shoppers uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on June 9, 2009; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No further action was ever listed: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor during the entire Congress [S4].
The bill's core mechanism was to authorize collective negotiation of card access fees between merchants and payment-system providers, with a judge panel as a backstop rate-setter [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Visa, Mastercard, and the banks that collect interchange fees on card transactions, who kept the existing fee structure untouched because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Card Fair Fee Act of 2009 in the Senate on June 9, 2009 [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 9, 2009 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Credit card issuers and networks
against.role: Visa, Mastercard, and the banks that issue their cards
against.what_they_did: Opposed collective negotiation of interchange fees, the same industry coalition that fought Durbin's later interchange regulation.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so its partisan shape cannot be measured from the record; the fight it anticipated was largely merchants versus banks rather than Democrats versus Republicans.

industries.note: They charge merchants a fee for access to their payment systems and set the terms merchants must accept. Lower, competitively set fees would cut directly into that revenue stream [S3].

Issuers collect most of the interchange fee on each card sale. The bill's cost-based standard for setting fees would reduce that income, and issuers could shift part of the loss to cardholders through higher annual fees or fewer rewards [S3].

Stores of every size pay a percentage of every card sale in interchange fees. Joint negotiation or judge-set fees would directly lower one of their largest operating costs, a saving that could reach shoppers through prices [S3].

industries.industry: Small banks and credit unions under $1 billion in assets
industries.note: The bill lets the judges set alternative fee schedules for small issuers regulated by the National Credit Union Administration or with under $1 billion in assets, softening the hit to community lenders [S3].
